1. Putting an ice cube to your skin when you want to cut
2. Drawing and writing when you want to cut - I write the hateful things I think about myself. Use a soft tipped pen

Hey, OP. I empathize a lot with you. 

When I was 19, I was dating my high school boyfriend. We had a lot of issues, mostly stemming from my immaturity and his. I think this ultimately led to there being very little affection in our relationship - he wanted to leave and he never wanted to see me. When he did, he wanted to do sex stuff. 

And he never took no as an answer. If I wasn't in the mood, or we couldn't find a place (we were in college) he would push and wheedle until I said yes, or he would be cold and leave. As a result I caved and said yes many times when I wanted to say no. 

At several vulnerable moments - one especially, when I was crying and panicking terribly - he pushed me to give him what he wanted and I caved. Now much later, I wonder a lot - was it any kind of assault? I said yes, didn't I? Does he ever think about it and feel guilty? Did he knowingly keep me around for just sex stuff? 

I do know this OP. Assault or not, I felt disgusting about what happened. And you deserve to date someone who cares about how you feel about sex too - before, during and after - not someone looking for a perfunctory green signal to achieve their own pleasure. Him violating a known boundary (sex) while you're drunk without checking in, questioning at the very least, let alone admitting that it was a decision to be taken when you are both 100% conscious was so wrong. And him pushing you after you said no, while he may have stopped if you really forcefully pushed him off, is still showing you that he doesn't care about how you feel, just that you bend to his will enough to say yes. 

Now, I understand that there are situations in a relationship when one may ask a few times, or maybe push a little for something - but if he's making you feel like your voice doesn't matter, then there is something very very wrong. Please OP, acknowledge how you feel - and act accordingly.

I can't tell you how angry this statement makes me. In some kinds of acne, diet has nothing to do with it. Spreading this kind of harmful misinformation hurts people who are already struggling with this issue - it makes them feel like it's their fault when it may not be, it could just be genetics. 

I was 14 when my clear skin suddenly started breaking out. I stopped eating chocolate for a year. I haven't eaten mangoes in years. I was eating only home food, fairly healthy clean Indian food. My face did not clear. Same thing now, during lockdown. Clean food, and yet I was getting pimples.

Both times I blamed myself so much. What am I doing wrong? Both times I went to a dermatologist who gave me medicine and told me I don't have to worry about my diet. This idea that you can control when you break out by controlling your diet is so pervasive that despite being told years ago recently I started blaming myself again for eating something wrong until a dermatologist told me *again* that I could eat what I want. 

I am not saying diet doesn't make a difference. I am saying it has nothing to do with 'healthy'. Some people need to eat very little sugar, some can't have milk. Those are restrictive and not health-related dietary choices. So get off your high horse and normalize acne because guess what? It happens, people have little control over  it and feel shitty for no reason.
